NASA's Near-Earth Asteroid (NEA) Scout project was used as an example to demonstrate the integration. A model for the small satellite was created in Cameo Enterprise Architecture, a well-known tool for employing SysML. The value model was created using Matlab and then integrated with Cameo.

The NEA Scout is a cube satellite (CubeSat) being developed by NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC), Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), and NASA Langley Research Center. The CubeSat is proposed to fly as secondary payload on the Space Launch System (SLS) Exploration Mission 1 (EM-1) to analyze and study near-earth asteroids (NEAs).

The expected mission duration is 2.5 years during which it will target a number of pre-identified targets to measure the physical properties of the asteroids to address certain key strategic knowledge gaps (SKGs). The satellite will be a standard 6U CubeSat with a maximum mass of 14 kg and will primarily employ commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components [25]. The Scout proposes to employ solar sail propulsion.

citations.quote: A detailed model of the structure and functionality of the Scout CubeSat was created in Cameo. The structural breakdown of the CubeSat into different systems is shown in Fig. 4. A block definition diagram (BDD) was used to represent this breakdown. In addition to this system level BDD, additional BDDs were created for different subsystems to represent each in detail and avoid cluttering in the system level BDD.

Other diagrams, namely activity diagrams, sequence diagrams, requirements diagrams, use case diagrams, sequence diagrams, and parametric diagrams were created to represent different functionalities of the system. These diagrams represent different views of the system that the stakeholder could use to enhance her understanding of the system. Examples of a BDD, a use case diagram, and a sequence diagram created for the Scout are shown in Figures 4, 5, & 6. These SysML diagrams are useful in representing system behaviors, understanding flows and system couplings, as well as in identifying emergent behaviors not anticipated during the initial phases of concept generation and conceptual design. Such a visual representation of the system also facilitates understanding of complex systems and variable relationships that may otherwise be difficult to comprehend. The variables and parameters of the system, including design variables, attributes, and physical constants, among others, are represented as value properties. Value properties may be characterized as variable type real, boolean, complex, integer, number, or string depending upon the nature of the parameter being represented. SysML also provides the designer with the ability of customizing value properties definitions.

The model was initially coded in Matlab to check for model feasibility. Each subsystem was coded to output the attributes associated with that subsystem. An analysis file was created to confirm convergence to a design. The outputs from this file were the total cost, total benefit, and total mass of the satellite. Total cost and benefit were direct inputs to the value model. A separate file was created to determine the value of the Scout, with total cost and total benefit being inputs to this file. The value model was then used to optimize and the optimal set of design variables for the satellite was found.

The constraint described in the problem statement states that the total mass of the CubeSat cannot exceed 14 kgs. This requirement originates from regulations governing small satellites. Due to this pass or fail regulation it is difficult to incorporate the preference into the value model as this regulation is a step function, driving benefits to zero if violated. Since the problem consisted of discrete design variables, it was decided to use Genetic Algorithm (GA) as the method of optimization [29]. Matlab's built-in GA optimizer was used.

citations.quote: Note that the value model used in this paper was of a very low fidelity. As such the values in Table 1 do not predict reality. The goal of this paper was to understand the integration of value models and SysML. Future work will involve higher fidelity, more realistic value models. These values were then used as a reference to compare the results obtained when the value model was integrated with SysML.

In order to integrate the value model into the SysML model, different parametric diagrams were created for the different subsystems to calculate the attributes associated with each subsystem. Parametric diagrams function by means of constraint blocks. These blocks are used to define the mathematical operations expected to be performed by the system or the function to be executed. Cameo version 18.4 (used in this research) provides 16 different language options to choose from to define the constraints, including JavaScript, Matlab, Mathematica, SQL, and English. In this paper, JavaScript was used to represent the constraints.

One of the main drawbacks of using this approach is the need for extremely large number of diagrams for calculating the variables. The number of diagrams increases with the size of the system. If a subsystem requires evaluation of a large number of variables in order to calculate the outputs needed by the value model, the number of constraints would be large. This is due to one constraint generally being associated with each variable. The consequence of this is an extremely cluttered parametric diagram due to all of the constraints being represented. Evidence of this clutter is seen in Fig. 8 that represents a high-level visualization of the parametric diagram for the ADCS subsystem. Another drawback observed was that parametric diagrams are only useful in performing simple mathematical calculations and are not yet fully equipped to handle complex computations in Cameo's SysML. For example, it was not possible to output an array using a parametric diagram. The activity diagram of Fig. 7 was used to circumvent this issue. Another drawback was that Cameo's SysML did not recognize a number of Java functions. Examples of functions not recognized were $ \log_{1 0} $ and 'for' loops. When implemented in Cameo the $ \log_{1 0} $ function call resulted in a return of a natural log evaluation. SysML did not work well with 'for' and 'if' loops either. The 'if' loops had to be replaced with 'switch' cases.

Building an optimization algorithm in SysML is not only time consuming but also will require significant modifications in order for the code to execute properly. Thus, the value model was not completely implemented using this SysML approach. Overall, this approach was arduous and would be recommended only in case of simple models that do not require complex mathematical operations.

The system model was first created in Matlab, with each subsystem coded to output the associated attributes. Other Matlab computations included an analysis to bring all the subsystem attributes together to evaluate the two system level attributes (total benefit and total cost), an evaluation of value of the system (profit), an optimization algorithm, and evaluation of the constraint (total mass).

In the constraint block that was created, shown in Fig. 9, the 'Matlab' language option was selected, and the function was copied from the Matlab file. The authors believe that this issue is due to conflicts between certain versions of Cameo and Matlab. Successful integration was achieved using a different version of Cameo than version 18.4 previously mentioned as well as a different version of Matlab. Another drawback of this approach was the inability to have array inputs in SysML. The default input for Matlab's optimization algorithm is in the form of arrays for the lower and upper bounds of the design variables and for the indices of the integer variables. The default code had to be tweaked so that the arrays were broken into separate input variables. This increased the number of input variables causing the parametric diagrams to be cluttered. The same was true for the output arrays. There is no straightforward method of having SysML output arrays. This approach is also not as detailed as the purely SysML approach, as most of the computational work is being done 'behind the scenes' in Matlab and we can generally only view the inputs and the outputs of the system.

Overall, although there were certain challenges and disadvantages associated with implementing this approach, it was considered to be easier than the pure SysML approach. Since SysML is not recommended for complex mathematical calculations, it was better to let Matlab handle that part and use SysML to understand the other system functionalities. The ability to view the system through different diagrams could help in understanding system properties such as the tradeoffs occurring within the system, related to the value model. Also, it was possible to successfully complete the integration of the value model with SysML using this approach because of the ability to perform an optimization through Matlab.

Since SysML is still evolving, future work will explore the usability of the pure SysML approach. Further investigations will explore the library of SysML functions to determine better means of implementing value models in SysML. Since the main focus of this paper was to explore the challenges associated with integrating value models with SysML, a very simple value model was used. Future work will involve forming a more realistic value model involving the time value of money and integrating it with SysML.

One of the benefits of this approach was that it was easier to understand the functionalities of the system due to the way SysML has been designed. The ability to view the system through the different diagrams helps improve understanding about the system [30]. Through the activity and parametric diagrams, it should become easier for the SysML user (e.g. designers, managers, top-level stakeholders) to get a feel for the system's functionalities and couplings. This is where SysML could have an edge. As SysML evolves and gains capabilities its ability to integrate value models with complex systems will improve.
